_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 580 words, six questions in text order: detail, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase and a final question linking the ending to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: Behind the seams
subtitle: Every week, costumes from a dozen theatres arrive torn, stained and missing buttons at Ruth Abara's tiny workshop in Leeds. Sam Doyle went to see how she puts them back together.

cards.text: At first glance, Ruth Abara's workshop looks like the morning after a very strange party. A Roman soldier's tunic hangs next to a wedding dress with a split down the back. A pair of enormous pantomime trousers lies across the table, waiting for new elastic. There are jars of buttons sorted by colour, a strong smell of steam from the iron, and a headless mannequin wearing a king's cloak at a slightly unsteady angle. 'People think a costume is made once and that's it,' Ruth says. 'Actually, a costume in a long-running show has a harder life than most of the actors.'
cards.question: What point does Ruth make about theatre costumes?
choices: They are usually designed to be worn only once.
They often cost more than the actors are paid.
They are more difficult to make than ordinary clothes.
They suffer a great deal of damage during a show's run.
cards.highlight: a costume in a long-running show has a harder life than most of the actors
cards.why: A costume 'has a harder life than most of the actors'. The idea that it is 'made once and that's it' is what other people wrongly think.

cards.text: She is not exaggerating. A dancer in a musical may spin, kneel and slide across the stage in the same jacket eight times a week for a year. Sweat rots the fabric under the arms. Quick changes, done in thirty seconds in the dark at the side of the stage, rip zips and tear off hooks. Ruth once received a ballgown that had been caught in a revolving stage, and she still has the photographs. She shows them to me with obvious pleasure, the way other people might show off pictures of a holiday.
cards.question: What does the writer suggest about Ruth and the damaged ballgown?
choices: She enjoyed the challenge of such a difficult repair.
She was upset by how badly it had been treated.
She believes revolving stages are dangerous.
She kept the photographs to prove she was not to blame.
cards.highlight: She shows them to me with obvious pleasure
cards.why: She shows the photos 'with obvious pleasure', like holiday pictures, so the job was a happy memory. Nothing shows she was upset or needed to defend herself.

cards.text: Ruth trained as a tailor in a menswear shop, making suits for bank managers, and admits she found the work dull. Theatre was a happy accident. A friend who worked as a stage manager rang her in a panic an hour before a first night, because the leading actor had torn his coat. Ruth did it in the dressing room, with the actor still wearing it. 'He had to stand completely still while I sewed,' she remembers. 'He said it was the best acting he did all week.' Within a month, three other theatres had her number.
cards.question: What does 'it' refer to in 'Ruth did it in the dressing room'?
choices: making a suit for a customer
calming her friend down
mending the actor's coat
performing on the first night
cards.highlight: Ruth did it in the dressing room, with the actor still wearing it.
cards.why: She did the repair 'with the actor still wearing it' and sewed while he stood still, so 'it' is mending the coat. The suits belong to her earlier, dull job.

cards.text: The hardest part of the job, she says, is that nothing can look repaired. An audience in the front row must not see a patch, and an actor must be able to move as freely as before. She hands me a white shirt and challenges me to find the place where it was torn. I examine it for several minutes, under a lamp, and fail completely. She turns it inside out and shows me a patch the size of my hand. 'Twelve hours,' she says. 'Nobody will ever know, which is exactly the point.'
cards.question: Why does the writer describe searching the white shirt?
choices: to admit that he knows very little about sewing
to show that Ruth's repairs are meant to be invisible
to suggest that Ruth's repairs take too long
to explain why theatres prefer white costumes
cards.highlight: Nobody will ever know, which is exactly the point.
cards.why: He cannot find a patch 'the size of my hand', which proves Ruth's point that 'nothing can look repaired'. The twelve hours are worth it to her, not a complaint.

cards.text: Theatres are rarely wealthy, and Ruth's prices reflect that. She could earn far more making wedding dresses, and every few months someone tells her so. She has also turned down a job with a film studio. 'Film costumes get worn for a few days and then go into a warehouse,' she says. 'Theatre costumes have to survive. I like things that have to survive.' She admits that she sometimes works until midnight before a big opening, but she does not seem to mind. For Ruth, the job is less a way of making a living than a labour of love.
cards.question: What does the writer mean by 'a labour of love'?
choices: work that leaves you physically exhausted
work you do as a favour for friends
work you would give up if you could
work done because you care about it, not for the money
cards.highlight: the job is less a way of making a living than a labour of love
cards.why: She charges little, refuses better-paid work and 'does not seem to mind' late nights, so she does it out of love. Long hours alone do not explain the phrase.

cards.text: Before I leave, a courier arrives with a large bag from a theatre in Manchester. Inside is a gorilla costume with one arm almost completely torn off. Ruth looks at it the way a doctor might look at an interesting patient, then lifts it carefully onto the table, beside the Roman soldier and the wedding dress. 'Matinee on Saturday,' she reads from the label, which also says PLEASE HURRY in capital letters, and reaches for her scissors. It occurs to me that the strange party in her workshop never really ends. The guests just keep changing.
cards.question: What does the writer mean by his final comment?
choices: There will always be new costumes arriving for Ruth to repair.
Ruth's workshop is too untidy to work in properly.
Ruth enjoys entertaining visitors from the theatres.
Some costumes stay in her workshop for years.
cards.why: The 'strange party' takes us back to the opening image of the workshop, and the gorilla is just the latest 'guest'. The guests change, so costumes do not stay for years.
